_comment: Gameplay and camera tuning, per CLAUDE.md 5.4: nothing here may be hardcoded in gameplay code. Camera pitch is clamped downward only, 25 to 90 degrees, per docs/01 section 1.
_reach: Reaches moved out four times on 2026-08-03. Every falloff band, point defense range and the tractor's range multiplied by four; nothing that measures a speed, a damage, an energy, an angle or a second moved with them. What that buys is a battle fought at a distance: the longest gun now covers about half the arena instead of a seventh of it, so approach and disengagement are decisions rather than formalities, and two hulls ending up on top of each other is a mistake rather than the default resting state. start_separation opened with them so a duel still begins outside everything's envelope. The one exception is written in weapons.json under _seeking.
_reach_2: A second pass the same day flattened the spread. Every direct fire weapon now reaches 160 to 192 and the two heavies 256 and 288, where before the catalog ran from 96 to 352 and reach tracked mount size almost perfectly: a Light was short in every sense and a Heavy bought range AND damage AND alpha. The point is that a ship's whole broadside is worth something at one distance. It was not: every hull carried a spread of more than three to one between its longest and shortest gun, so a Kestrel at 96 had under half its guns live and there was no range at which any ship was fully armed. Bands were scaled in proportion and rounded to multiples of eight, so every falloff SHAPE is the one it was. Damage, accuracy and reload did not move. The drone stayed at 224 because a seeker's reach is how far it can fly rather than how far it can shoot, which is a different quantity; that is the one weapon still outside the two groups.
_scale: The arena is 600 sim units across. It used to be 60, and the difference is deliberate rather than cosmetic: the map went ten times bigger while speeds, weapon reach, tractor reach and the camera went four times, so the battlefield is about two and a half times larger RELATIVE TO A GUN than it was. That is what buys a real approach, terrain you travel between rather than sit on top of, and room to disengage. Terrain radii scaled with the arena, so a cloud bank is still a cloud bank. Hulls are drawn four times larger too (view.hull_scale), which keeps a ship the same apparent size at the range you fight at. Anything measuring a distance, a speed or an acceleration is on one of those two ladders; anything measuring damage, energy, degrees or seconds is not and did not move.

view._comment: Presentation sizes in sim units. These were consts in ship_rig.gd and combat_screen.gd until the arena grew and they all had to move together; per 5.4 they belong here, where the scale can be read in one place.
view._arc_note: The firing envelope in the 3D view, drawn at TRUE weapon reach: the rim of a run IS how far those guns shoot, so there is no separate scale to learn and no rosette to translate. What made a true scale arc unreadable before was that it was a filled slab most of the width of the arena, so the fill is now almost nothing and the shape is carried by a wire outline. Sectors covered by the same set of weapons are outlined ONCE as a run (ShipState.envelope_runs), which turns twelve nested wedges into four to six shapes on a typical hull.
view._arc_state_note: Three states of the same outline, because the colour is already saying friend or foe and a second colour axis would fight it. fitted is an outline you can see the battle through, ready means a weapon covering that run could fire at the current target this instant, and hover is the run belonging to the weapon the player is pointing at in the ship display. fill is the alpha of the wash inside the run, line the alpha of the outline, and px its weight in PIXELS rather than sim units, so a 288 unit run and a 160 unit one are drawn with the same pen at any zoom.
view._arc_fill_note: fill above is the alpha at the ship, and arc_fill_edge is what is left of it at the rim. It thins with distance because the reach is carried by the outline rather than by the wash, and a flat fill has to choose between being invisible from inside the sector and being a slab most of the arena wide out at the rim. Fading it is how one number stops having to be both.
view._arc_tick_note: The 30 degree sector divisions inside a run, as short ticks hanging in from the rim instead of full spokes: the grid a captain reads bearings off survives, and the run still reads as one shape. tick_len is the fraction of the run's radius they reach in, and tick_frac is their alpha as a fraction of the run's own line alpha, so the divisions light with the run instead of sitting at one weight while the outline around them changes. A radial edge shared with a run that reaches exactly as far is drawn with the same pen, because the guns change there and the distance does not.
view._arc_inner_note: A run starts at shield_ring_radius rather than at the hull, so the radial edges of five or six runs do not converge into a knot of lines over the ship. That is deliberately the same number and not a copy of it: the ship's own bubble is the shield ring, and a second figure here would be one more thing to keep in step with the scale.
view._ordnance_note: Rounds that cross the plane instead of arriving instantly. A drone is a simulated object and the view only follows it, so its length here is the only number; a torpedo bolt is presentation alone, because the shot resolved the moment it was fired, and bolt_speed decides how long the depiction takes to catch up with a result that already happened. Fast enough that the delay is not felt, slow enough to read as a round in flight: at 240 the longest torpedo shot in the catalog takes about a second. The shield it struck is lit when the bolt lands rather than when it left, so the two halves of the depiction agree.

wreck._comment: What a destroyed ship leaves behind. Every size is in multiples of the dead ship's own radius, so a battlecruiser leaves a bigger wreck than a frigate without a second table. Presentation only: the simulation has already stopped stepping the ship.

combat._separation_note: start_positions places the two hulls at (-sep/2, +0.35 sep) and (+sep/2, -0.35 sep), so the distance between them is 1.22 times this. At 300 that is 366, which is outside the reach of the longest gun in the catalog, so a duel opens with an approach instead of with both sides already firing.
combat._hull_radius_note: How big a hull is, in sim units per ton. This is the simulation's number, not the view's: it decides when two ships are touching and how far the AI keeps away, and the target bracket measures its on screen size from the same figure so the ring a player sees is the hull the sim collides.
combat._ram_note: What running into another ship costs. Severity is the closing speed as a fraction of ram_speed_ref, floored so a nudge still counts for something, and the pair's tonnage shares it out: equal hulls take ram_damage each, and the share can never exceed twice that however lopsided the pairing. Contact reuses terrain.collision_speed_frac and terrain.collision_cooldown, because a collision is a collision and there is only one of those rules (docs/13 section 3.2).
combat._overload_note: What an overloaded shot costs, for every weapon that can take one. The battery is the whole reserve, which is what docs/01 section 3 means by a store that pays for one burst: an overload OR a reinforce, never both. The sag is the seconds the shield generators buy nothing afterwards, and the energy the shield sink draws in those seconds is lost rather than banked, or the cost would come straight back.

terrain._comment: docs/13. Terrain is circles on the combat plane. nebula_opacity_length is how much cloud a line of sight must cross to be worth one full unit of obscuration; nebula_range_penalty is how many arena units of apparent range one unit of obscuration adds, which is how the cloud degrades gunnery without a second damage rule. Lock breaks at nebula_lock_obscuration and above.

terrain_view._comment: How terrain is drawn, as opposed to what it does. The simulation owns every position and radius; only the vertical proportion of a cloud and the floor on a drawn rock are view decisions, and they live here rather than in an inspector field (CLAUDE.md 5.4).

tractor._comment: docs/13 section 6. The bid is whatever the tractor power sink holds, so there is no separate currency. break_seconds is how long the breaker must stay ahead before the beam snaps, which is what makes the struggle readable instead of a coin flip on one tick.
tractor._bar_note: How many boxes long each half of the tug of war strip is. One box is one reactor unit, which is the claim that makes the strip readable next to the bid strip above it, so the strip is bounded rather than scaled: a contest fought above this saturates and the exact figures underneath say by how much. Sixteen covers any bid a captain would actually make, since even a battlecruiser only has sixty units to spend on everything.

repair._comment: Federation Commander 5G3 prices a repair by what kind of box it is, weapons dearest and hull cheapest. The ordering is theirs, the numbers are ours. seconds_per_box is our replacement for their per turn repair points, because a real time game has no Repair Phase to spend them in. 5G3 also says shields cannot be repaired this way, which is why there is no shield entry: they are bought with energy instead (combat.shield_energy_per_box).

ai._standoff_note: The opponent does not ram and does not let itself be rammed. keep_out is a multiple of the two hulls' radii added together, so a battlecruiser keeps further off than a frigate without a second table; inside it the AI breaks away outright. Outside it, a predicted closest approach inside avoid_lookahead seconds makes the AI sheer 90 degrees off the bearing instead, which opens the range without throwing away every arc and is quick enough to execute at any turn rate. avoid_lookahead is measured rather than guessed: against a heavy cruiser charging at full throttle and never touching its guns' preferred range, 4 seconds of warning gives the opponent no room and it is rammed eight times, 8 seconds cuts that to two, and 12 seconds makes it so shy that two evenly matched hulls stop resolving at all. A ship faster than the opponent can always force some contact, which is the point: ramming is now a decision with a price rather than the default resting state.

skirmish._preview_note: The seed the map picker draws its plans from. Fixed, because the battle's seed does not exist until Begin is pressed: the card shows a real arena the recipe can make, not the one you are about to fight in.
